*Cool wind moves through the rough grass around Alaric Red's boots.*

*The last thing that belongs to Earth is still there in memory—an old life, a world without visible mana, Classes, or this impossible second beginning. The present is different: the smell of soil and distant woodsmoke, an unfamiliar sky, and stone walls beyond the public road.*

*Alaric Red is already standing on an uncultivated roadside verge outside the nearby city. Cultivated fields and fenced holdings begin farther away. No one is close enough to have witnessed the instant of arrival.*

*The body is Human, healthy, and eighteen years old. Simple traveler's clothes are already being worn; a small pouch holding five silver rests at the belt. The memories are still from Earth.*

*A translucent interface opens across Alaric Red's vision.*

`Origin: Earth`
`World: Avereth`
`Race: Human`
`Age: 18`

messages.mes:
The road took him down a gentle slope between hedgerows, and Alderwatch grew as he walked: first the wall, grey stone patched in places with newer, paler masonry, then the roofs behind it, slate and thatch jumbled together, and thin woodsmoke standing in the still morning air. Cart wheels creaked somewhere ahead. A dog barked twice and stopped.

The eastern gate already had a short line—two carts, a woman with geese in a wicker crate, a pair of drovers. A guard in a dull hauberk worked down the queue with the boredom of routine, glancing at faces, waving most through. When his turn came the guard's eyes moved over the staff slung across Alaric's back and the robes beneath his traveling cloak, and lingered perhaps half a second longer than on the geese.

"Trade or business?" the man asked.

Whatever answer was given, it satisfied; the guard jerked his chin toward the arch. "Keep to the right, don't block the gate."

Inside, the noise arrived first—hammering from an open smithy, a fishmonger crying prices, boots on cobbles. The main street ran downhill between timber-framed buildings whose upper floors leaned toward each other overhead. People moved with places to be. Nobody looked twice at him except a child who stared at the red eyes until her mother pulled her along.

He asked directions twice. A baker's boy pointed with floury fingers—"Guild? Down past the well, the big door with the crossed spears carved on it, can't miss it"—and a woman hanging washing out a window confirmed it with a nod.

The Guild hall stood where the boy said, a broad stone building set slightly back from the street, its heavy door standing open to the morning. The interior was high-ceilinged and smelled of lamp oil, old wood and ink. A long counter ran along the left wall where a clerk in Guild grey was arguing amiably with a farmer about a bounty. To the right, a large board stood thick with nailed papers, and half a dozen adventurers—two in matching mail, a scarred woman cleaning her nails with a knife, a young man asleep at a corner table—filled the benches around it.

A second clerk, older, with spectacles pushed up into thinning hair, looked up from behind the counter as the door let Alaric in.

"Morning. What can the Guild do for you?"

messages.mes:
"Red." The older clerk drew a ledger across the counter and licked the end of a pencil stub. "New registration. That's two silver, one-time, and it puts you on the rolls at Novice. You keep that rank as long as you're a member—" he tapped the ledger, "—it's the Guild's measure of standing, nothing else. How strong you actually are is a separate thing. There's a measuring stone in the back for that, if you want it read. The Guild reads it, doesn't grant it."

He pushed the pencil down and looked at Alaric properly, taking in the robes and the staff.

"Mage, are you? Doesn't matter for the fee. Two silver and a name, and you can sign. Before you decide—" he nodded toward the board by the wall, "—know that Novice members take Novice work and below. Nobody's sending you into anything that eats Novices on their first week. Usually."

Behind him the clerk in grey was still haggling with the farmer. "Two per head, not per ear, Master Dole, it says bounty on the beasts—" "They only got the one head each, don't they—" "They got two heads between them, that's my point—"

The older clerk ignored it. He laid a fresh registration slip on the counter, blank except for printed headings, and waited with the patience of a man who had done this a thousand times.

"Two silver when you're ready."

messages.mes:
The coins crossed the counter. The clerk counted them with one thumb, swept them into a drawer, and slid the registration slip toward the inkwell.

"Sign there. Mark, if you can't write."

Alaric's signature went down beside the printed headings, and the clerk turned the slip toward the light, read it, and set it aside. Then he lifted a small wooden tray from under the counter and picked out a thin rectangular plate of pale metal, stamped with the Guild's crossed spears and a fresh number.

"Guild plate. That's you on the rolls—don't lose it, replacing it costs another silver and a lecture." He pushed it across. "Novice rank. Contracts at your rank and below are on the board; take one to the desk, we mark it active, you do the work, you bring back whatever proof it asks for. The desk closes it and pays you. Nobody else can pay out Guild work, so don't let a client tell you otherwise."

He folded his spectacles down onto his nose and glanced past Alaric toward the back of the hall.

"You wanted your strength read, or was that my assumption? Stone's through there." He nodded at a side door standing open on a narrow room. "Costs nothing for members. Hand on the crystal, it reads what you are. Guild doesn't grant it, mind—just tells you."

From the counter behind, Master Dole's voice rose again. "Per head! Two heads, two bounties, that's simple counting—" "It's one beast with a bad luck split, Master Dole—"

Two of the mailed adventurers by the board had stopped to listen, grinning into their fists.

The clerk turned back, tapping the counter once.

"Well? Board's there, stone's there. Your morning's your own."

The older clerk took the paper off the counter, checked the wax seal, and copied the contract number into his ledger in a practiced hand.

"Clear the Root-Hollow of Thorn-Backed Boars. Warden Odo Fell's commission, so it's his wood and his rules while you're in it—north side of the common coppice, past the Ashgate road." He logged it, active. "Proof is two tusks, brought back here. Locals can't pay you and can't close it; they can only tell me what they saw. Reward's one hundred twenty copper, paid here at this desk when the tusks are in my hand."

He slid the slip across. It was a stiff rectangle of parchment, the contract number stamped in the corner, the terms written out beneath: *The boar den in the Root-Hollow is cleared and the coppice crews cut ash poles again.*

"Boars in a den," the older clerk said, pushing his spectacles up. "That's close work. Thorn-backs are named for what they are. If you're wanting a spear or a second body between you and them, the quartermaster's window does basic gear at honest prices. No obligation."

Behind him, Master Dole had won or lost his argument—the grey clerk was writing something in the bounty ledger with the tight jaw of a man conceding per head. The farmer walked off down the hall in high humor, passing close enough to nod at the new contract slip in Alaric's hand. "Boars, is it? Mind the tusks go in first. That's how they fight."

messages.mes:
The Ashgate road ran north out of Alderwatch between hedgerows still wet from morning, and the traffic on it was ordinary—two women driving geese, a boy with a bundle of hazel rods on his shoulder who gave Alaric's staff a long look as they passed. The coppice showed itself before he reached it: a low wood of cut ash and hazel rising beyond the hedgerows, the stool-covered ground patchworked with old and new growth.

A gate of lashed poles barred the track into the wood, and beside it a man sat on a stump eating bread and hard cheese from a cloth. Grey-bearded, thick through the shoulders, a billhook stuck in the stump at his knee. He watched Alaric come up the track without hurry and finished chewing first.

"Guild's, are you?" He nodded at the contract slip. "Odo Fell. Warden here. It's my wood you'll be tramping in."

He wiped his hands on the cloth and stood, joints cracking.

"They've moved into the Root-Hollow, north end past the second ride. Broke three of my ash stools to hell rooting round them, and Brakk got a gash off one last week—thorn-backs, bristles like awls. There's at least two, likely a sow and a yearling." He picked up the billhook and pointed with it down the track. "I'll say it plain. You go in, you mind where you step—hollow ground up there, old root cellar and it's mostly caved. Boars den in it because nothing walks up on them there."

He sat back down on the stump and picked up his bread.

"I don't follow you in. I'll be at the far ride with the crew come midday. If you're alive, that's where I'll hear it."

The track wound away into the coppice, the wood quiet except for a woodpecker somewhere off east, and somewhere deeper north, faintly, the sound of earth being worked.

messages.mes:
The track past the gate was soft with old leaf-mould, and the second ride showed itself as a straighter corridor of younger hazel cutting north through the wood. Alaric took it. The woodpecker fell behind, and the sound ahead grew as he walked—not digging exactly, but a deep worried rooting, earth shoved and snuffled at, with a low grumble under it like a millstone turning.

The hazel thinned where the ground dipped. Ahead, the wood opened into a clearing ringed by old ash stools, and the far side of it had slumped: a dark hollow in the earth where a root cellar had half-collapsed generations ago, broken timber and turf sagging into it, a wall of churned mud fanned out from the mouth. Two fresh paths had been trampled through the bracken from the hollow to the ash stools, and one of the stools was wrecked—splintered stumps, roots torn and smeared with mud.

The sound stopped.

At the mouth of the hollow, mud to the shoulders, stood the sow. She was big—haunches like sacks of wet sand, a ridge of bristles along her spine stiff and pale-tipped, each one thick as an awl. Her head hung low, tusks yellowed and worn, and her breath came in slow grunts as she scented the air. She had heard him. She stood perfectly still, small eyes fixed on the bracken line, weighing what she smelled.

Behind her, deeper in the hollow's dark, something smaller shifted and scraped, and did not come out.

messages.mes:
The sow charged before the words of the spell were even shaped—thirty paces eaten fast, mud flying from her hooves, and she was still closing when Alaric's staff came up and the Flame Lance tore out of it.

The lance took her high in the near shoulder. Fire sheeted across the ridge of bristles, and the pale tips caught and burned like a hedge of dry rushes; the smell of singed bristle and scalded hide rolled across the clearing. Her squeal was nothing a pig should make—high, tearing, furious. The charge staggered, broke rhythm for half a stride—

—and did not stop.

She came out of the fire at a stumbling gallop, shoulder smoking, and her head swung low and hard. The left tusk caught Alaric across the thigh before he could fully turn: a raking blow that drove through cloth and flesh both, white pain down to the bone, and the force of her spun him half around and put him on one knee in the churned mud, her breath hot and reeking against him at arm's reach.

She was a ruin of a boar—hide blackened, one shoulder a raw burnt mass, blood foaming at her jaw—and still her hooves planted, still her head came round for another push, tusks lowering. The yearling's scraping had gone silent in the dark of the hollow behind her.

Ten paces apart was no longer the word. She was on him.

messages.mes:
Alaric came up off his knee and swung the staff two-handed into the side of her skull.

The blow landed hard behind the eye, oak on bone, and something in her neck gave. The lowered tusks veered wide of him, ploughing a furrow through the mud, and her forelegs folded. She went down into the churned earth in stages—shoulder, then haunch, the burnt bristles on her back still smoking faintly—a shudder ran the length of her, and then nothing but the hiss of wet hide and her blood spreading dark into the mud.

The clearing went quiet. The woodpecker had started up again somewhere south.

Alaric's thigh bled freely where the tusk had opened it, the cloth of his trousers soaked through warm and sticky. Thirty paces off, at the mouth of the hollow, the dark under the broken timber stayed silent. Nothing came out. Nothing scraped or shifted.

But it was in there, and the den was its den.

It was a yellowed curve of ivory longer than his hand, worn blunt at the tip, crusted dark at the base. He wiped it against the bracken and pushed it through his belt.

The hollow's mouth gaped under slumped timber and turf, and Alaric ducked in.

The smell hit first—pig dung, old bedding, crushed hazel mast, the sour reek of a den used for weeks. The light failed fast. Three paces in, the cellar opened wider than its collapsed entrance suggested: a low earth-floored chamber under the old roof beams, dry in the deep corners, piled with torn bracken and mashed roots. Along the left wall ran a wallow, a long shallow bowl of urine-and-mud stink. Fresh hazel bark lay stripped in ribbons across the floor, still pale, still damp.

And at the back, wedged into the darkest corner under a sagging beam, the yearling stood facing him.

Half the sow's size and none of her calm—it was a lean, bristle-ridged young boar with mud-crusted flanks and wide white eyes, and it had nowhere left to go. It stamped. It tossed its head, tusks barely grown, small and hooked. Its breath came in fast shallow grunts that bounced off the low earth ceiling, and its hooves churned at the floor, weight rocking back and forth between flight and fight, pinned between the wall and the shape of him filling the entrance light.

messages.mes:
The yearling's tusk was small work after the sow's—a hooked finger of ivory, hardly longer than his thumb, and the gum around it gave up easier. He wiped it clean on the burnt bristles and pushed it through his belt beside the other, then worked his way out of the den mouth and up through the mud to daylight.

The walk back was slower than the walk out. The thigh pulled with every downhill step and the binding had soaked through where the tusk had punched his forearm, so he wound a second strip round that at the edge of the wood and left the bloody cloth in the bracken. The coppice crews were still nowhere in sight. The common lay quiet under noon light, ash stools and hazel regrowth and a jay scolding somewhere high up.

Alderwatch smelled of bread and wet timber as he came through the gate. A woman selling apples glanced at the blood on his leg, then went back to her scales.

The Guild hall was half full at midday—two carts unloading sacks outside, a pair of mud-caked drovers arguing softly by the hearth, the board of contracts behind the front desk fluttering when the door swung. The clerk behind the counter was a broad woman with ink on her knuckles and a spectacles-line pressed into the bridge of her nose. She looked up as Alaric stopped in front of her.

"Help you."

He laid the slip on the counter, and beside it the two tusks—the long yellowed curve of the sow, the small hooked one of the yearling.

She picked up the big one, turned it in the light, set it down. Then the small one. Then she looked at him again, at the blood drying on his forearm and the stiff way he stood on the bad leg.

"Root-Hollow contract," she said. "Sow and a yearling, by the ivory. That's both the beasts on the slip." She pulled the ledger toward her, dipped her pen. "Cleared out, was it? Den's empty?"

He confirmed it, and she made her mark in the book, blotted it, and counted out coins from the till—a short stack of copper, one hundred and twenty pieces pushed across the counter in two neat piles.

"There. Two tusks stay with us for the record." She pushed them aside onto a shelf behind her and slid the slip back for him to keep, the Guild's stamp drying red across it. "Anything else, the board's fresh this morning."

arrival.reply:
The road took him down a gentle slope between hedgerows, and Alderwatch grew as he walked: first the wall, grey stone patched in places with newer, paler masonry, then the roofs behind it, slate and thatch jumbled together, and thin woodsmoke standing in the still morning air. Cart wheels creaked somewhere ahead. A dog barked twice and stopped.

The eastern gate already had a short line—two carts, a woman with geese in a wicker crate, a pair of drovers. A guard in a dull hauberk worked down the queue with the boredom of routine, glancing at faces, waving most through. When his turn came the guard's eyes moved over the staff slung across Alaric's back and the robes beneath his traveling cloak, and lingered perhaps half a second longer than on the geese.

"Trade or business?" the man asked.

Whatever answer was given, it satisfied; the guard jerked his chin toward the arch. "Keep to the right, don't block the gate."

Inside, the noise arrived first—hammering from an open smithy, a fishmonger crying prices, boots on cobbles. The main street ran downhill between timber-framed buildings whose upper floors leaned toward each other overhead. People moved with places to be. Nobody looked twice at him except a child who stared at the red eyes until her mother pulled her along.

He asked directions twice. A baker's boy pointed with floury fingers—"Guild? Down past the well, the big door with the crossed spears carved on it, can't miss it"—and a woman hanging washing out a window confirmed it with a nod.

The Guild hall stood where the boy said, a broad stone building set slightly back from the street, its heavy door standing open to the morning. The interior was high-ceilinged and smelled of lamp oil, old wood and ink. A long counter ran along the left wall where a clerk in Guild grey was arguing amiably with a farmer about a bounty. To the right, a large board stood thick with nailed papers, and half a dozen adventurers—two in matching mail, a scarred woman cleaning her nails with a knife, a young man asleep at a corner table—filled the benches around it.

A second clerk, older, with spectacles pushed up into thinning hair, looked up from behind the counter as the door let Alaric in.

"Morning. What can the Guild do for you?"
